topics.topic: Classification and increment semantics for refused-attempt and lockout counters
questions: Are refused sign-ins and lockouts one counter or two, can one request increment multiple counters, how are nonexistent sessions separated from out-of-set projects, and which other refusals are excluded?

What increments each counter, whether overlapping refusals increment one or several kinds, whether a lockout event and its refused sign-ins are counted separately, and whether viewing resets or acknowledges anything?
What is one attempt, how are requests matching several kinds classified, whether a lockout is counted once or per refused request, and whether concurrent attempts must update the count atomically?

quotes:
After the first release is assembled, with the changes R0-93, R0-94 and
R0-96 planned, Registry counts refused attempts in memory from its start and
shows them to the owner on the first page after sign-in, with the instant of
the start and of the latest of each kind: refused sign-ins and lockouts;
calls on the service API with a token Registry does not know; calls whose
token does not allow the operation or class asked; and, apart from these,
Kernel's agent-authority calls refused for a session or a project outside
its set, the weakest sign, since a revocation by the owner yields them too.
judgement.why: Counter classification, increment, concurrency and reset semantics are rules owned by State 2.

topics.topic: DPIA screening authority, recorded conclusion, deadline, and consequences
questions: Who performs and approves the screening, what recorded output constitutes completion, by when must it finish, and what happens if it concludes that a DPIA is required?
What is the actual screening conclusion, who is authorised to make it, where is it recorded, and what happens if the conclusion is instead that a DPIA is required?
What is the actual screening decision, who records it, and what happens to production start and import if the screening instead concludes that a DPIA is required?

quotes:
The screening and, when needed,
the DPIA are the governance's, platform-wide (Explicit exclusions); this
specification's matrix (`sources/privacy_requirements_20261123.md`) is their
section on the measures Registry takes.

So Registry's
production start and its one import (R0-79) do not wait for the screening,
which is made now, in parallel.
judgement.why: Authority, records, deadlines and consequences of the governance screening are operational governance notes outside Registry's State 0 product boundary.

topics.topic: Delivery and maintenance of writer guidance for safe room names and aliases
questions: What exact text and interaction teach the rule in the owner interface and manifest, who changes them, and what happens if either surface still carries the old description?
Who injects the governance instruction into every agent session before the manifest description is changed, how is its presence verified, and what happens when it is absent or ignored?

Before the manifest and owner-interface descriptions are changed, what concrete component supplies the rule to every agent and owner writing a room name or alias, and what happens if those instructions are absent or stale?

quotes:
The writers learn the rule
where they write: the owner from the governance and the owner interface, the
agent from the description of the room name and the alias in Registry's
manifest record (R0-78). That description is changed with the changes
planned after the first release is assembled (R0-93, R0-94); until then the
rule binds the owner, and the agent through the governance's instructions to
it.
judgement.why: Exact owner-interface interaction and manifest wording belong to the later public-surface design.

topics.topic: Detection and rejection of standing approvals inside collection maps
questions: Who detects that a node is inside such a map, who prevents the standing approval, and what observable failure occurs if the owner attempts to grant one?
Who detects that a node executes inside a collection map, who refuses a prohibited standing approval, and what happens if the owner grants one despite the governance rule?
Which component detects that a Registry-writing node is inside a map and prevents or refuses the standing approval, and what observable failure occurs when one is attempted?

quotes:
The owner's approvals are the bound on how much the agent writes; Registry
sets no count of rooms, pointers or requests. The governance's rule is that
no standing approval is given to a node that writes to Registry inside a map
over a collection.
judgement.why: The text makes the prohibition an organisational governance rule, not a Registry detection or rejection promise.

topics.topic: Legacy objects-folder cleanup, verification, ordering, and effect of import
questions: Who performs and verifies this cleanup, what evidence proves the agent has lost access, and may the screening conclusion or continued processing be relied on before that verification?
Who performs the cleanup, what exact access and copies must be removed, how is completion verified, and may production start or import complete before it succeeds?
Does importing itself remove or disable every legacy copy and access path, or does that require the separate cleanup and retirement actions?
Must production start or import wait for removal of the agent's access to the earlier objects folder, and what verifies that the cleanup succeeded?

quotes:
It holds once the owner's earlier machine no longer gives the agent the
objects folder (the cleanup step of the home server's move).

The processing already goes on: the legacy v1 instances hold the real data
(R0-79). The import moves it into one protected home, out of every agent's
reach, with erasure and restriction; it lowers the risk. So Registry's
production start and its one import (R0-79) do not wait for the screening,
which is made now, in parallel.

Production Registry starts without waiting for the other services. From its
start Registry holds the customer's personal data as R0-80 says and gives each
service what it needs to stop keeping copies. Each service removes its own
customer records and copies in its own case — PresuPro's project snapshots and
database backups, Cabinet's package of projects, the legacy instances once
retired (R0-79).
judgement.why: Cleanup execution, verification and deployment ordering are operational matters, while the texts already separate import from later removal of legacy copies.

topics.topic: Machine-readable data-subject copy contents, schema, format, and exceptional states
questions: What exact machine-readable format, schema, field set, identifiers, metadata, encoding and failure result must the owner produce?

What exact data belongs in the copy, which values count as data provided by the customer, what schema and format are used, and how are erased, restricted, archived and issued-document data represented?
What records and fields must the copy contain, in what machine-readable format and schema, and how are absent, restricted, erased, retained or unreadable parts represented?

quotes:
The machine-readable copy is the owner's,
assembled from those reads. Registry gains no operation for it now.

The records of processing, the DPIA screening and, when needed, the DPIA
itself, blocking under LOPDGDD Art. 32 (R0-91), the procedure that answers
a data subject's request (R0-93), incident response and the other organisational measures. They are
kept as platform-wide governance — Registry, Cabinet Kernel, Cabinet,
PresuPro, Client Portal and the external AI providers — outside this case,
judgement.why: The copy is a governance-produced artefact rather than a Registry operation, so its assembly format and exceptional-state handling belong to operational notes.

topics.topic: Product contract for the customer/project review and JSON-download operation
questions: Is this operation part of the product promise, and if so what records, archived projects, anonymised projects, artifacts and errors does it include?
Is this operation part of the product, and if so what triggers its delivery and what exact page and JSON contract does it provide?
Is the combined page and JSON-download operation part of the product, and if so what are its authorization, selection, output and failure semantics?

quotes:
A read-only owner operation that gathers a customer with every project
naming it, as one page and a JSON download, is a candidate change once the
first release is assembled; adopting it is a new owner decision here.
judgement.why: The combined page and download are expressly only a candidate and are not part of the product until another owner decision adopts them.

topics.topic: Propagation and recorded completion of corrections, restrictions, and erasures across recipients and copies
questions: When Registry corrects, erases or restricts data already held in Portal's offline projection, who communicates or applies that change, by what trigger, within what time, and what happens while Portal is offline?
How is the owner told that follow-up is required, how are the affected recipients and copies identified, and what observable record proves that correction or erasure was completed?

What identifies every affected recipient, issued document, offline projection and legacy copy after a rectification, restriction or erasure, and what records that each required correction or notification was completed or lawfully omitted?

quotes:
What still holds a value is followed by the owner, by the governance's
procedure, after each such change:

- Client Portal's offline projection (R0-39) is Portal's; whether Portal keeps
  one and how it follows a change is stated in Portal's case;
judgement.why: Recipient identification, completion records and offline follow-up are assigned to governance operations and Portal's own case, not Registry's State 0 behavior.

topics.topic: Registry blocking applicability, scope, duration, access, and final destruction
questions: Which Registry values, if any, must enter blocking instead of being erased, what starts and ends blocking, and what must Registry return while they are blocked?
Which Registry values, if any, must enter blocking instead of erasure, for how long, and what operations and final destruction apply to each?
Which Registry values require blocking, when does blocking begin, how long does it last, who may access blocked values, and what exact action destroys them when it ends?

quotes:
Registry offers no blocking. Whether any value it holds — a customer's
contact or fiscal data, an object's address — must be blocked after erasure
rather than erased is a question for the legal review of the governance
(Explicit exclusions). Until it is answered, erasure in Registry erases
(R0-06, R0-60) and the governance records where blocked data lives — today the
documents a service issued, which an erasure in Registry does not rewrite
(R0-80). A legal answer that some Registry value must be blocked is a new
owner decision here.
judgement.why: Current behavior is unambiguously erasure with no Registry blocking, and any future blocking requires a new State 0 decision.

topics.topic: Release dependency and activation timing for refused-attempt counters and their display
questions: Does counting activate independently, only when all referenced changes are adopted, or in one atomic release; and which R0-93 change is meant when its gathering operation is only a candidate?
Is counting contingent on all three named changes, what precise release must include it, and are attempts before that release intentionally unobservable?
Which release must introduce the counters and sign-in display, and may production operate after the first release without this measure?

quotes:
After the first release is assembled, with the changes R0-93, R0-94 and
R0-96 planned, Registry counts refused attempts in memory from its start and
shows them to the owner on the first page after sign-in, with the instant of
the start and of the latest of each kind: refused sign-ins and lockouts;
calls on the service API with a token Registry does not know; calls whose
token does not allow the operation or class asked; and, apart from these,
Kernel's agent-authority calls refused for a session or a project outside
its set, the weakest sign, since a revocation by the owner yields them too.

A read-only owner operation that gathers a customer with every project
naming it, as one page and a JSON download, is a candidate change once the
first release is assembled; adopting it is a new owner decision here.
judgement.divergence: One implementation activates counting in the first post-assembly release independently; another waits until all referenced changes, including any intended R0-93 candidate, are adopted, and the owner notices whether attempts appear after sign-in.
judgement.why: The counter promise is tied to an undefined assembly milestone and ambiguously to planned changes, one of which contains a non-adopted candidate.

witness.initial: The first release has been assembled, but no new decision has adopted R0-93's candidate combined download operation.
events: A maintainer releases the next Registry version.
The owner signs in and opens the first page.
outcomes: The page shows the refused attempt because counting activated independently after assembly.
The page shows no attempt because counting was deferred until all referenced changes were adopted together.

topics.topic: Retention-period configuration keys, units, defaults, validation, and change timing
questions: What configuration keys, units, defaults and validation rules represent each period, and what does the page do when a period is absent, invalid or changed?
What configuration fields and units define each period, which data kind each applies to, what defaults and validation apply, and when configuration changes take effect?
Which period keys, units, allowed values and defaults exist, what happens when a required period is missing or invalid, and when does a changed period take effect?

quotes:
After the first release is
assembled, it gains a read-only review page in the owner interface: the
customers whose relationship ended, and the archived projects archived, longer
ago than periods the owner sets in the configuration from the schedule.
judgement.why: Configuration validation, defaults, effective timing and due-date comparison are rules owned by State 2.

topics.topic: Whether R0-91 through R0-99 can be closed while key decisions remain deferred
questions: How can these questions be closed when R0-91, R0-93, R0-94, R0-97 and R0-99 expressly leave blocking, a customer-download operation, retention-page design, durable security logging and write-count enforcement to later owner decisions?
How can these questions be closed while the same decisions leave Kernel correlation, blocking scope and design, post-release operations, durable logging and the DPIA conclusion to later decisions?
Where are the expressly deferred legal, product, trace-correlation, blocking, post-release and DPIA decisions tracked if this unit declares that no question remains open?

quotes:
A read-only owner operation that gathers a customer with every project
naming it, as one page and a JSON download, is a candidate change once the
first release is assembled; adopting it is a new owner decision here.

A durable log of security events, kept apart from the audit log with its own
period, is reconsidered — by a new owner decision here — when Registry gains
a second human principal who signs in to it, or a surface reachable other
than through the owner's VPN and the WireGuard channel (R0-39, R0-48). Until
then the count shown at sign-in is the measure.

A count enforced by Registry is reconsidered, by a new owner decision here,
if standing approvals for such writes become needed.
judgement.why: These passages explicitly make the cited matters prospective candidates or conditional new decisions rather than unresolved obligations of the currently accepted product frame.

topics.topic: Backup erasure deadline, start event, removal mechanism, and restoration behavior
questions: What is that period, when does it start, what operation removes or expires the value, and what is observable if a backup is restored before expiry?
What is the actual maximum period, when does it start, and does loss occur through expiry, overwrite, deletion or restoration filtering?

quotes:
Third, whatever the second step did, it deletes every kept
   backup made more than 30 × 24 hours before the instant this step starts,
   one cutoff for the whole step — a backup made exactly 30 × 24 hours before
   it is kept.

While the daily runs succeed and each ends before the next 03:00, an
   erasure reaches the backups by the first
   run after the last backup holding the erased values is more than 30 × 24
   hours old (rule 4) — at
   most 31 days after the erasure — and a failed or missed run lengthens that
   by the days until a run succeeds. A restore loses the changes made after
   the backup it uses; Registry bounds neither how long a run takes nor how
   old the newest kept backup may be.

Registry has no restore operation (R0-89). A store the owner puts in
   place of a lost one starts as any store (A17 rule 5) — by the release that
   made its backup, or by a later one after that release's own store
   migration — and begins its own history from the backup: numbering
   continues from its last number (A15), and a store without the migration
   closure accepts the import (A16).
judgement.why: State 2 A18 specifies rolling deletion, its timing and failure extension, and the behavior of a restored backup.

topics.topic: Fields and contextual changes that bind or invalidate an exact standing approval
questions: Which request fields and contextual facts make an approval exact, and is it invalidated by a flow-version change, node change, project change, session change, record revision or manifest-contract change?
Which request fields, project and session identities, flow and node versions, request id, and displayed values are bound by an exact approval, and which change invalidates it?

quotes:
Each such write of the
agent waits for the owner's approval of its exact request, unless the owner
gave that flow version a standing approval for the node (K-08).
judgement.why: The canonical approval binding and invalidation fields are part of Cabinet Kernel's operation and flow contract.

topics.topic: How a locked-out owner observes and distinguishes lockout-related refusal
questions: How can the owner learn why sign-in is refused while locked out, and when is the first successful opportunity to see the counters if attempted access continues?
How can the owner learn that a lockout caused sign-in refusal while the owner remains unable to sign in, and what observable failure distinguishes lockout from a wrong credential?

quotes:
Today Registry refuses them and keeps no trace (A14 rule 2),
and the sign-in lockout of A13 rule 3 is runtime state the owner never sees,
so a locked-out owner cannot tell why the sign-in is refused.

After the first release is assembled, with the changes R0-93, R0-94 and
R0-96 planned, Registry counts refused attempts in memory from its start and
shows them to the owner on the first page after sign-in, with the instant of
the start and of the latest of each kind: refused sign-ins and lockouts;
judgement.why: The text expressly says a locked-out owner cannot distinguish the cause and that the future counters are visible only after a successful sign-in.

topics.topic: Registry-to-Kernel trace correlation key and execution-link contract
questions: Must every Kernel trace record contain Registry's request id, what uniqueness scope applies to it, and which operation can follow a Registry room or pointer to the matching node execution?
Must Kernel record Registry's request id as a unique searchable correlation key, and what uniqueness, retry and cardinality rules bind that key?
What Registry fact, if any, links a pointer withdrawal to the Kernel execution that performed it?

quotes:
What Registry keeps is the link from its records to that trace: the request
id a room's create carries (State 1 M03) and the publisher, with its session,
and the request id of a pointer's publish (M05, R0-88). Both are facts
Registry already holds; this decision adds none. Whether Kernel writes the
key it gives as that request id into its trace record, so that a room or
pointer leads to exactly one node execution, is Kernel's to state in its
case; until it does, the link is one-directional. Neither Registry nor the
platform gains a separate control module.
judgement.why: The text deliberately guarantees only one-directional correlation, delegates Kernel trace-key cardinality to Kernel's case, and names no withdrawal request-id link.

topics.topic: Required release and objective delivery milestone for the retention review page
questions: Is the review page already required, or must implementation wait for another decision; and what event objectively means that the first release is assembled?
What event precisely means the first release is assembled, in which release must the page exist, and what happens if that release is deployed before the page is designed?

quotes:
Registry keeps erasing nothing on its own (R0-60). After the first release is
assembled, it gains a read-only review page in the owner interface: the
customers whose relationship ended, and the archived projects archived, longer
ago than periods the owner sets in the configuration from the schedule. The
owner acts on each with the existing actions. If the legal review answers that
some value must be blocked, blocking enters the same change, as one mechanism
with the review page. The design of both is decided then, by a new owner
decision here.
judgement.divergence: One implementer treats “it gains” as requiring the page in the next release after assembly; another waits for the stated new owner decision and omits it, which the owner notices during retention review.
judgement.why: The passage promises the page after an undefined milestone while also saying its design awaits a later owner decision.

witness.initial: The first release has passed its tests, but no later owner decision has designed the review page.
events: A maintainer prepares and deploys the next release.
The owner performs the periodic retention review.
outcomes: The release includes a review page because the promise activated after assembly.
The release omits the page because implementation waits for the new owner decision.

topics.topic: Retention review page contents, eligibility explanations, boundaries, and failure behavior
questions: What fields, ordering, boundary comparison, pagination and eligibility explanations does the page show, and does it also show audit entries due for erasure?

Does the page include already erased or anonymised records, restricted customers, records currently covered by a lawful retention ground, and records exactly on the deadline; what information and failure state does it show?

After the first release is

judgement.why: Page fields, ordering, pagination, boundary presentation and failure rendering belong to the later owner-interface surface design.

topics.topic: State model and implementation behavior for a future Registry blocking mechanism
questions: Is the review page allowed to ship without blocking, and what state model, actions, reads, destruction rule and migration apply if blocking is required?
What blocking state, transitions, permissions, review-page behavior, audit behavior and terminal destruction action will be implemented if the legal review requires blocking?

quotes:
If the legal review answers that
some value must be blocked, blocking enters the same change, as one mechanism
with the review page. The design of both is decided then, by a new owner
decision here.

Registry offers no blocking. Whether any value it holds — a customer's
contact or fiscal data, an object's address — must be blocked after erasure
rather than erased is a question for the legal review of the governance
(Explicit exclusions). Until it is answered, erasure in Registry erases
(R0-06, R0-60) and the governance records where blocked data lives — today the
documents a service issued, which an erasure in Registry does not rewrite
(R0-80). A legal answer that some Registry value must be blocked is a new
owner decision here.
judgement.why: No blocking mechanism currently exists; if legal review requires one, its entire state model and its coupling to the page require a new owner decision.

topics.topic: Trigger, limits, scope, and failure behavior for future Registry write-count enforcement
questions: What condition means standing approvals have become needed, and what limits, time window, scope and failure behavior would Registry enforce?
What condition establishes that standing approvals are needed, what room, pointer and request limits would apply, and is enabling such approvals forbidden until those limits are decided?

quotes:
The owner's approvals are the bound on how much the agent writes; Registry
sets no count of rooms, pointers or requests. The governance's rule is that
no standing approval is given to a node that writes to Registry inside a map
over a collection. A count enforced by Registry is reconsidered, by a new
owner decision here, if standing approvals for such writes become needed.
judgement.why: Current behavior has no Registry count and forbids the relevant standing approvals by governance; any future limits require a new owner decision.

topics.topic: Whether excluding special-category names is a system guarantee or writer-only policy
questions: Is preventing special-category data from reaching an agent a platform guarantee or only a writer policy that may fail, and what control handles a violating name before disclosure?
Is preventing special-category data from reaching the agent a guaranteed system behavior or only a writer obligation whose violation the system accepts and transmits?

quotes:
A room name reaches the agent and so its AI provider (R0-68), and the agent
may write one itself (R0-41). A name such as "bathroom for the wheelchair"
says something about the health of a person living there: data of a special
category (GDPR Art. 9), which the platform must not hand to an agent.

As in R0-68 and R0-90, this is a rule on the writer — the owner, and the agent
through Kernel — not a check of Registry: Registry cannot tell what a word
means, refuses no name for its content and searches no text for words; a
name that breaks the rule does reach the agent.
judgement.why: For the same accepted room name, one obligation forbids handing its special-category implication to the agent while the other requires accepting and returning it to the agent.

topics.topic: Controlled agent document intake and handling of prohibited values
questions: Who creates and controls that folder, how documents reach it without prohibited customer names or delivery addresses, what validates or reviews them, and what happens when a prohibited value is present?

topics.topic: Coordination and aggregation of data-subject answers from other services
questions: Which services must be queried, by whom, through which actions, and how are their results combined with Registry's answer?

topics.topic: End-to-end ownership and evidence for handling data-subject requests
questions: Who receives a request, verifies the requester and their authority, records its receipt and deadline, coordinates answers from all services, records partial refusal, and proves completion or failure?

topics.topic: Finding duplicate customer identities belonging to one data subject
questions: How does the owner find every Customer record and project about one data subject when recording the same person twice is allowed to create two unrelated Customer identities?

quotes:
The owner answers, within the period Art. 12(3) sets, by a
procedure the governance records, from the actions Registry already has:
'read a customer'; 'list projects' with the archived ones, whose items carry
`customer_ref`, to find the projects that name the customer; 'read a
project' for each, with its object and rooms; and 'list artifacts'.
judgement.why: Registry already supplies customer listing and per-customer reads, while subject identity matching across duplicate records belongs to the governance procedure that operates those actions.

topics.topic: Governance owner, governing artifact, synchronization, and release gate for required procedures
questions: Which named governance owner and artifact supplies these procedures to Registry's owner, how Registry-version changes are synchronized with them, and what blocks release when a required procedure is absent?

topics.topic: Governance-versus-Registry ownership of blocking responsibilities
questions: If R0-94 later adds blocking to Registry, which parts remain governance and which concrete state, actions, outputs and destruction behavior become Registry responsibilities?

topics.topic: Requester identity and representative-authority verification
questions: How does the owner establish that the requester is the data subject or an authorised representative before disclosing or erasing Registry data?

topics.topic: Runtime sharing and restart boundaries of in-memory counters
questions: Is the count per process, per worker, per Registry instance or shared across workers, and what exactly constitutes the start or restart shown to the owner?

topics.topic: Trigger, admissibility, event coverage, and retention for durable security logging
questions: What exact topology or principal change triggers reconsideration, must the durable log exist before that change becomes admissible, and what events and retention would it cover?

author_guidance: Before editing, identify the decision's owning state from the phase purpose, question_scope and layer obligations, then choose a disposition for each topic that awaits one.
fixed: repair a decision the owning state must make; do not add later-layer implementation choices merely to close a topic. Record the fix commit and review the changed text once.

carried: name the receiving layer and use --what to preserve the choice, its options and consequences, and the required guarantee every option must keep. Decide any guarantee owned here before carrying its execution onward.
accepted: explain why the remaining choice is permitted. Bring an unresolved product choice to the owner with its options and consequences; absence of a quoted requirement does not decide it.
contradiction and standard_violation take no disposition: repair the offending text in its owning state and review the change. Deterministic transition findings must also close through their checks.
